items.stem: Before compounding an oral suspension, the compounder discovers that the balance failed its accuracy check and that yesterday's ingredient weights cannot be reconciled. The finished suspension looks normal. What should happen next?

choices.text: Release the preparation because a visual inspection substitutes for quantitative controls.
choices.why: Incorrect. Appearance alone cannot establish accurate ingredient amounts when weighing equipment is unreliable.

choices.text: Hold the preparation and correct the weighing problem before release.
choices.why: Correct. Reliable measuring equipment and traceable execution are essential to compliant nonsterile compounding.

choices.text: Shorten the beyond-use date without investigating the ingredient weights.
choices.why: Incorrect. Changing the BUD does not repair a potentially wrong concentration.

choices.text: Delete the incorrect measurements from the record and retain only the final appearance.
choices.why: Incorrect. Removing data undermines traceability and does not resolve the failed balance check.

items.citation: 247 CMR 9.01(3); MA Board Retail Pharmacy Inspection Template (nonsterile compounding controls and records); applicable USP <795>
items.novelty_rationale: Focuses on a physical measuring-equipment failure rather than another USP numerical BUD memory test.

items.stem: A community pharmacy has classified a medication it stocks as a hazardous drug using its current hazardous-drug list. It ordinarily dispenses intact manufacturer-finished tablets under an assessment-of-risk program. An individual prescription now requires the tablets to be CRUSHED and mixed into a patient-specific oral suspension; staff propose using the same ordinary counter used for intact tablets and skipping additional containment because the drug has not changed. According to the Massachusetts Board's USP <800> advisory, which steps are appropriate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Treat crushing as equivalent to dispensing an intact tablet with no additional exposure assessment.
choices.why: Incorrect. Crushing changes exposure risks and triggers the Board advisory's hazardous-compounding discussion.

choices.text: Evaluate the hazardous-drug risk and apply the required containment controls for the crushing and compounding process.
choices.why: Correct. The advisory identifies HD crushing or capsule opening for compounded preparations as a containment-requiring situation.

choices.text: Conclude that USP <800> does not apply to community pharmacies as long as they do not prepare sterile products.
choices.why: Incorrect. The Board explicitly applies HD handling expectations to community pharmacies including nonsterile compounding.

choices.text: Ensure the designated responsible person and applicable work-practice, facility, and staff controls are in place.
choices.why: Correct. The Board advisory requires a formal HD program and designated trained responsible person.

items.citation: 247 CMR 9.01(3); MA Board Advisory USP <800> in Community Pharmacies (revised Feb. 3, 2022), pp.1-3; USP <800>
items.novelty_rationale: Distinguishes actual manipulation from intact dispensation without presenting alternative containment as an unconditional exemption.

items.stem: The pharmacy's periodic controlled-substance inventory is expressly taken AS OF CLOSE of business on Friday, not at opening. Before closing, staff received a case of controlled medicine and moved it to the secured prescription area. A separate bottle remains quarantined for a quality investigation but is still in the pharmacy's physical custody. Purchasing records also list medication ordered from a supplier that has not been delivered and is not under the pharmacy's control. Which counting decisions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Count the afternoon receipt that was physically on hand before closing.
choices.why: Correct. The close-of-business snapshot includes controlled substances under the registrant's control at that time.

choices.text: Count stock that a supplier has invoiced but that remains outside the pharmacy's possession or control.
choices.why: Incorrect. A mere undelivered purchase does not establish physical possession or control on the date of inventory.

choices.text: Include the quarantined controlled bottle still held under the pharmacy's control.
choices.why: Correct. On-hand inventory includes substances under registrant control, not only drugs available for dispensing.

choices.text: Exclude the afternoon receipt because it arrived after the pharmacy opened.
choices.why: Incorrect. An inventory taken as of close includes receipts already on hand by closing time.

items.citation: 21 CFR 1304.11(a),(c),(e) (on hand and opening/closing inventory basis)
items.novelty_rationale: Short evidence snapshot explicitly distinguishes ownership/control, received inventory, and inventory cutoff time.

items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy arranges delivery of a refrigerated prescription to a customer's workplace. The patient has not designated a receptionist or alternate pickup location as an authorized agent. When a courier arrives, the patient has left and the receptionist offers to store the sealed carton in an unrefrigerated drawer until the next afternoon. The courier has not transferred custody, and the pharmacy has a written procedure for failed delivery and temperature excursions. What should the courier and pharmacy do?

choices.text: Leave the sealed package, since the unopened seal alone proves patient delivery.
choices.why: Incorrect. A seal does not establish authorized receipt or protection from temperature-related degradation.

choices.text: Mark the package as delivered and ask the patient to collect it when convenient.
choices.why: Incorrect. The proposed handoff has not been authorized and no actual patient/agent delivery occurred.

choices.text: Keep custody and investigate safe redelivery.
choices.why: Correct. Pharmacy delivery procedures must protect product integrity and prevent unauthorized handoff.

choices.text: Store the package in a reception drawer and cancel the counseling offer.
choices.why: Incorrect. Uncontrolled overnight storage does not satisfy stability or authorized-delivery requirements.

items.novelty_rationale: Tests custody and temperature consequences of an actual failed delivery rather than ordinary mail-order permission.

items.stem: An inspection report cites two violations at a Massachusetts pharmacy, and the Board has given no alternative deadline. The manager proposes a general letter promising to 'improve compliance soon.' What does 247 CMR 9.25 require instead?

choices.text: Submit a violation-specific correction plan within 21 days.
choices.why: Correct. The regulation requires a specific written plan of correction for each violation within 21 days absent another Board deadline.

choices.text: Only an acknowledgment that the manager received the inspection report.
choices.why: Incorrect. Receipt acknowledgment does not satisfy the required deficiency-specific correction plan.

choices.text: Only a commitment to retrain staff, without dates or assignment of responsibility.
choices.why: Incorrect. The corrective plan must include an implementation date and responsible individual for each violation.

choices.text: No written response until an individual pharmacist faces disciplinary charges.
choices.why: Incorrect. Facility inspection correction and individual licensure discipline are distinct processes.

items.novelty_rationale: Uses a deficiency/plan-of-correction mini-document and 21-day facility deadline, not an individual discipline case.

items.stem: For a patient's prescription naming a particular reference biologic, the pharmacist checks the FDA's interchangeability classifications rather than relying on a wholesaler's marketing language. Product Y is an FDA biosimilar but has NO interchangeable designation for that reference product. Product Z is FDA-designated INTERCHANGEABLE with it. The prescriber has not given a written patient-specific prohibition against substitution, and the pharmacy has access to the patient's interoperable EHR. Which Massachusetts actions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Product Y qualifies for automatic substitution solely because FDA has found it biosimilar.
choices.why: Incorrect. Massachusetts substitution requires the legally recognized interchangeable relationship, not biosimilarity alone.

choices.text: Product Z may be selected under the interchangeable-biologic rule, subject to other requirements.
choices.why: Correct. FDA interchangeability qualifies a product for the statutory substitution pathway when no patient-specific written ban applies.

choices.text: No patient notification is needed if the prescriber receives a notice in the EHR.
choices.why: Incorrect. The statute requires notifying the patient or authorized representative in writing as well as prescriber communication.

choices.text: The substitution must be documented and communicated as required, including written patient notice.
choices.why: Correct. M.G.L. c.112 §12EE requires prescriber notification, written patient notification and a retained substitution record.

items.citation: M.G.L. c.112 §12EE(b)-(f); FDA Purple Book interchangeability classification
items.novelty_rationale: Actual source-table reading requires choosing interchangeable status, then satisfying distinct prescriber and patient notice obligations.

items.stem: During a shortage, Pharmacy A offers two transfers to Pharmacy B: one bottle to fill an already identified patient's prescription, and another bottle solely to replenish B's general stock. Which federal DSCSA distinction is correct?

choices.text: Both are excluded because all transfers between retail pharmacies are emergency transactions.
choices.why: Incorrect. The specific-patient-need exclusion does not extend to general stock replenishment.

choices.text: Neither is subject to any drug-transfer law because both pharmacies are licensed.
choices.why: Incorrect. The DSCSA exclusion is narrow and does not waive other applicable distribution or controlled-substance rules.

choices.text: The general-stock transfer is excluded, but the identified-patient transfer is a wholesale transaction.
choices.why: Incorrect. This reverses the statutory specific-patient-need exclusion.

choices.text: Only the identified-patient transfer gets the DSCSA tracing exclusion.
choices.why: Correct. FDA expressly distinguishes fulfillment for an identified patient from stocking in anticipation of future demand.

items.citation: FD&C Act §§581(19), 582(d)(1)(A)(ii); FDA DSCSA Product Tracing FAQ; other applicable CSA rules remain
items.novelty_rationale: Distinguishes actual identified patient need from inventory stocking, rather than repeating a general wholesale exemption.

qa_note: USP 795 full operative text not independently authenticated for C098; no disputed BUD numerics used. Board HD advisory directly corroborates C103. All options still require final source-ledger signoff.
